Average purchase cost needs units: four equal-cash purchases, four different prices

Four charts trace equal cash purchases into unit counts, ownership shares, average cost and final market value without treating a price average as an investment return.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Follow the dollars and units through four equal-cash purchases

Interactive planning lab

Total units after four purchases240.0
Purchase cost per unit · total cash / total units$16.67
Final market value minus total contributed cash$800

Original four-purchase bookkeeping illustration. The same positive CAD amount becomes available and is invested at each stated purchase date in one hypothetical unit class. Units are bought at the entered price, fractional units are allowed without limit, and none are sold. There is no starting investment, no initial lump sum waiting beside the schedule, and no claim that future contributions exist today. No fees, bid/ask spread, taxes, distributions, currency conversion, stock split, minimum lot or execution delay is modeled. Full precision is retained in calculations; displayed quantities and currency are rounded. Average purchase cost is total cash invested divided by units acquired, not the simple mean of the four price observations. Final value is calculated immediately after purchase four at that fourth price. Its difference from contributions is a dollar gain or loss, not an annualized return, a money-weighted rate, a strategy ranking or a tax adjusted-cost-base calculation. The path is an entered scenario, not historical performance or a forecast.

The central idea

Divide total purchase cash by total units acquired. A lower average cost than the simple mean of quoted prices is an accounting result, and does not guarantee a profit or prove one investment schedule is better.

01

Start with the cash bought and the units received

Buying the same dollar amount at regular intervals does not buy the same number of units. The price at each purchase date determines how many units that cash can acquire. An average of price observations therefore answers a different question from the average cost of the units actually owned.

Investor.gov defines dollar-cost averaging through equal portions invested at regular intervals. Its description explains the basic quantity effect: the same money buys more units at a lower price and fewer at a higher price. This guide uses that relationship for an accounting illustration, rather than predicting a benefit for a real investment.

The original example makes four purchases of CAD 1,000 each. Its entered prices are CAD 20, CAD 10, CAD 25 and CAD 20 per unit. All units belong to one hypothetical unit class, and fractional purchases are allowed. No fee, spread, tax, distribution or currency conversion changes the cash invested.

Each CAD 1,000 becomes available at its purchase date. The model does not begin with CAD 4,000 of cash held from day one or compare investing an existing lump sum immediately with holding it for later. Those are different funding assumptions addressed in the related timing guide.

02

Add unit quantities before calculating cost per unit

For each purchase, units acquired equal cash invested divided by price. The four purchases acquire 50, 100, 40 and 50 units. Together they cost CAD 4,000 and acquire 240 units.

Average purchase cost is therefore CAD 4,000 ÷ 240 = approximately CAD 16.67 per unit. Calculations retain full precision even though the displayed currency is rounded.

The first bar chart shows the different quantities directly. The CAD 10 purchase accounts for 100 units, twice the quantity bought by CAD 1,000 at CAD 20. The CAD 25 purchase accounts for only 40 units. These unequal quantities are the weights missing from a simple average of prices.

The mechanics assume every order executes fully at its entered price and can buy arbitrary fractions. Actual products may have order sizes, dealing times, spreads, commissions or fractional-unit restrictions. Those conditions can change both the cash used and the quantity received.

03

Cash shares and unit shares have different denominators

Every purchase supplies 25% of the total cash because all four cash amounts are equal. The unit shares are approximately 20.83%, 41.67%, 16.67% and 20.83%. Each list separately adds to 100% before rounding.

The grouped chart keeps those denominators apart. A purchase can supply one-quarter of the money and more than two-fifths of the units. A percentage is interpretable only after its denominator is named.

The simple mean of the four prices is (20 + 10 + 25 + 20) ÷ 4 = CAD 18.75. It gives each date’s price one equal weight. It does not give each acquired unit one equal weight, so it is not the average cost of the 240 units.

The unit-weighted price calculation does reconcile with the cash ledger: (20 × 50 + 10 × 100 + 25 × 40 + 20 × 50) ÷ 240 is CAD 4,000 divided by 240. Adding price observations without those unit weights describes the observations, not the purchase cost.

04

The harmonic mean is an identity under these limited assumptions

When the same cash amount B is invested at four positive prices, acquired units sum to B × (1/p1 + 1/p2 + 1/p3 + 1/p4). Dividing the total 4B cost by that quantity cancels B.

The resulting cost per unit is 4 ÷ (1/p1 + 1/p2 + 1/p3 + 1/p4), the harmonic mean of the prices. With positive prices it cannot exceed their arithmetic mean, and it equals that mean when all four prices are identical.

This mathematical comparison does not establish that an investor earned an excess return or chose a better trading plan. The two means are statistics calculated from the same executed purchases. An alternative strategy comparison would need consistent available resources, dated orders, waiting cash and the same endpoint.

Changing the cash purchase amount scales quantities and dollar results without changing this frictionless cost-per-unit statistic. It still changes the household money committed. Equal averages do not make two differently sized positions equally important to a financial plan.

05

Mark all accumulated units at the final price

At the fourth price of CAD 20, the 240 units have a market value of CAD 4,800. Compared with CAD 4,000 of contributed cash, the final dollar difference is positive CAD 800.

The line chart shows the cumulative cash and the marked position after each purchase. After the second purchase, 150 units at CAD 10 are worth CAD 1,500, below the CAD 2,000 already contributed. Buying additional units does not remove the loss on earlier units when the current price is lower.

Change the fourth price to CAD 5 and the result becomes a loss. The four purchases then acquire 390 units, with a final market value of CAD 1,950 against CAD 4,000 of contributions. Having more units and a lower average cost does not ensure that the final price is above that cost.

The dollar gap is not an annualized, time-weighted or money-weighted return. Cash arrived on four dates, and the tool does not assign calendar spacing for a rate calculation. It also does not calculate cash available after a sale, tax payable or a tax adjusted cost base.

06

Use the accounting before choosing an investment schedule

For a real record, reconcile each trade’s cash, execution price and units with its confirmation. Keep fees, distributions, currency conversions and corporate actions in the appropriate ledger. Do not combine incompatible unit classes or unadjusted prices across an event that changes unit counts.

FINRA’s discussion distinguishes investing money as it becomes available from intentionally delaying investment of cash already held. It also notes that repeated transaction costs and waiting cash can affect a schedule. These implementation issues remain outside the frictionless four-purchase identity.

Neither the chosen price path nor the fact that its harmonic mean is lower than its arithmetic mean supplies evidence about future market direction. A plan must still consider the investment’s suitability, diversification, time horizon, cash needs and the ability to keep funding purchases.

The useful accounting sequence is concrete: record the cash invested, calculate and add the units, divide cost by units, then mark the entire position at the valuation price. The four charts preserve those steps so that a price average, unit quantity and dollar gain are each given the meaning their calculation supports.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. All prices and purchase amounts are original hypothetical scenarios. No security, historical price series or expected return is represented. Fractional units and frictionless execution are assumed. The example does not calculate a tax cost base or compare alternative strategies. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
